extracted.intended_audience: poets, translators, literary critics, editors, and readers of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive and critical guidance on composing, translating, arranging, and editing poetry (epic, elegy, lyric), plus general principles of diction, meter, and editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic subject — personal interest and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem, to be epic, must have a personal interest; otherwise the hero's interest will be merged in the interest for the event. In general, 'an epic poem must either be national or mundane.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is so overwhelmingly public (e.g., destruction of Jerusalem) that no single hero can retain personal interest, it is unsuitable for the highest kind of epic. Choose a subject that allows a personal/heroic focus, or make the epic explicitly national (addressing a people) or mundane (universal human concerns, as Milton did). Example: Milton chose a mundane theme (Adam and Eve) to secure universal interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting divinity — plain scriptural diction
rubrics_metrics.description: When God is represented as directly acting as Creator, adopt the simplest and sternest language of the Scriptures; avoid 'poetic diction' or amplification in direct divine action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's judgment: use scriptural plainness for the Voice/Word of the Lord. In dramatic addresses (e.g., Father to Son) one may 'slip in' more affectionate or poetic language, but the direct acts of the divine should retain objective, simple phrasing. Use anthropomorphism prudently to serve poetic necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegy — subjectivity and reference to the poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Elegy is the form of poetry natural to the reflective mind; it may treat any subject but not for itself — always and exclusively with reference to the poet himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal themes are sorrow and love; elegy presents everything as lost/gone or absent/future. It is the opposite of the Homeric epic (which is external and objective). When writing elegy, keep the focus inward: events/things are meaningful insofar as they affect the poet's feeling or meditation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyric ode — subjective yet presentational
rubrics_metrics.description: The true lyric ode is subjective but delights to present things as actually existing and visible, though often associated with past memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike elegy (which makes things remote/absent), an ode should use subjectivity to illumine present, visible images while linking them to feeling or recollection. Preserve vivid presentational imagery even while the speaker remains inwardly engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation — match meter to the original's feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: In translating metrical verse, choose a target-language metre that answers in feeling to the original metre (e.g., what metre in English will answer to the Greek elegiac couplet?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider not only formal equivalence but the 'feeling' and rhythm the original conveys. Meter choice should aim to reproduce the emotional and rhythmic effect rather than rigidly copy syllable counts. Example concern raised: how to render Greek elegiac couplet feeling into English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial restoration ('Poetical Filter') — remove whimsical or dated passages
rubrics_metrics.description: One may create improved 'wholes' by omitting parts of old lyrical poems where whim, bad taste, or fashion prevailed over genius, and possibly inserting a single corrective line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editing can restore otherwise-exquisite material that current readers neglect because of a few incongruous passages (example: many Wordsworth poems). Thoughtful omission or minor insertion may increase accessibility and popularity without falsifying the poet's best work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of a poet's works — chronological order
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronological order is preferable for arranging a poet's works to allow readers to watch the progress, maturity, and decay of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other categorical divisions may be 'inadequate' and can destroy the interest that arises from seeing a poet's development. Arrange collected works to show evolution over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and word-formation — favor concise words; avoid excessive agglutination
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid artificial compound-agglutinated words where the language's stage of formation makes them awkward; concise, shorter words often produce superior poetic diction (as Virgil exemplified by rejecting many compounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare counts of words per line across poets (e.g., Virgil vs. Lucan or Statius); prefer clarity and shorter words unless common usage sanctions a compound. Be wary of forcing Grecian agglutination onto languages unsuited to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve connective particles and rhythmic appoggiaturas in style
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical Greek oratory originally used many connective particles and appoggiaturas of time (small rhythmic ornaments); later Alexandrian writers lost these features, resulting in more compressed lines and fewer temporal ornaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aiming for the rhetorical fullness and connective flavor of earlier oratory/poetry, preserve these small connective elements and temporal appoggiaturas; avoid over-compression that strips rhythmic nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic distinction — beauty vs. expression or interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is distinct from expression or interest; it is an immediate presence (tranquil and one), whereas the 'interesting' disturbs and is disturbed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing, recognize that something can be beautiful without serving expression or conveying interest. Aim for that immediate presence when appropriate rather than confounding beauty with mere effect or significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as compression — 'il più nell'uno' (more-in-one)
rubrics_metrics.description: True poetic imagination includes a 'modifying faculty' that compresses several units into one whole ('il più nell'uno'); lacking this, poems become disjointed bright eminences separated by dark, unintelligible ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for unity: synthesize multiple elements into a single, comprehensible whole. Avoid producing isolated brilliant lines without connective, integrating imagination—Landor is cited as an example lacking this faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone for travel/military accounts — avoid sentimentalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers who write accounts of their travels should spare readers sentiment; the magazine-introduced 'cant' of sentiment should be avoided in favor of the practical manner of older captains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate pragmatic models (e.g., Dampier) rather than sentimental or fashionable emotionalizing. Keep descriptive travel prose grounded, factual, and unsentimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial accessibility for older texts (e.g., Chaucer)
rubrics_metrics.description: To revive an older poet's popularity, provide aids (a competent metrist marking syllable pronunciations), glossaries, or minor modernization (replacing obsolete words with other words from the same author) so readers can access rhythm and sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: mark final è and other syllabic endings, supply glosses, or make careful textual substitutions drawn from the author's corpus to preserve tone while restoring intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve original voice and formal innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: An author's distinctive language and formal inventions (e.g., Shakespeare's blank verse and unique diction) should be recognized as original creations rather than forced into the mold of contemporaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When editing, teaching, or critiquing, avoid trying to 'support' an author's diction by comparison to others; acknowledge and preserve the unique syntactic and prosodic devices that constitute an author's voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive self-reference — separate 'I' from 'Me'
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers (especially young writers) should remove excessive self-centeredness; 'I am me' is a fault in both grammar and intellect—avoid making the self the undue center of discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate perspective and propriety: ensure that statements and narratives have reasons and connections beyond mere self-assertion. Check for overuse of self-referential phrasing that isolates the writer from broader concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument tone — practice what you preach about tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing in favor of tolerance, the writer should treat sincerely held beliefs of others with respect or indulgence rather than adopting an intolerant tone; don't produce 'intolerant books on tolerance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In polemical or persuasive writing on sensitive matters, model the moderation you advocate. Avoid lampooning or trivializing other faiths or sincerely held convictions; argue with historical empathy and fair representation.
